body.title: The Vineyards Above Manarola
body.subtitle: Where ancient terraces meet the sea, one winemaker tends the same vines his grandfather planted

body.quote: The muretti a secco don't just hold back the earth—they hold back time itself
body.leftContent:
From my kitchen window in Manarola, I can see Marco Capellini's trenino making its morning climb. The small motorized track carries empty crates up the steep terraces, disappearing into the green tangle of vines that cling to these improbable slopes. By evening, those crates will return heavy with Bosco and Albarola grapes, the same varieties his family has grown here for five generations.

These terraced vineyards—carved into cliffsides so steep you can barely walk them without grabbing onto something—represent one of the most labor-intensive wine traditions in the world. No tractors. No shortcuts. Just hands, stone walls, and the kind of patience that only comes from truly loving a place.
body.rightContent:
The dry-stone walls, muretti a secco, date back eight centuries. They were built without mortar by farmers who understood that certain things are worth the work. Today, Marco is one of maybe forty winemakers still tending these terraces above Manarola. It's not romantic. It's backbreaking, expensive, and there are easier ways to make wine.

But when you taste what comes from these sun-drenched slopes—especially the amber-gold Sciacchetrà that takes four months to make from dried grapes—you understand why some traditions refuse to disappear.

body.markdown: In March, when the morning fog still clings to the hillsides, Marco begins pruning. Each vine gets individual attention—a conversation in cuts and choices about which canes to keep, which to remove. The Vermentino vines wake early, their sap already rising. By April, the first green shoots appear, tender and hopeful against the gray stone of the ancient terraces. This is when Marco worries most. A late frost could devastate a year's work in a single night. But the sea moderates the temperature, and these particular slopes catch the morning sun in a way that offers protection. The old farmers knew what they were doing when they chose this land.

July heat turns the terraces into an oven of stone and light. The muretti a secco absorb the sun all day, then radiate it back through the night—a natural climate control system that helps the grapes develop their distinct mineral character. Marco checks for mildew, thins the clusters so each grape gets enough sunlight, and rides the trenino up and down these impossible slopes half a dozen times a day. Tourists photograph the colorful village below, unaware that the real story is happening in these silent rows above. The Bosco grapes swell slowly, developing the crisp acidity that makes them perfect for the local white wine. This is the waiting time, when there's little to do but trust the process and maintain the walls.

body.alt: Hand holding freshly harvested wine grapes during vendemmia harvest season
body.caption: Photo by Maël BALLAND on Unsplash

body.markdown: Late September brings vendemmia—harvest time. This is when the entire valley mobilizes. Marco's extended family arrives from Genova. Neighbors help neighbors. The work starts early, before the sun gets too hot, and the trenino runs constantly, hauling plastic crates filled with Bosco, Albarola, and Vermentino down to the cantina. The harvest for regular wine happens first, quick and focused. But for Sciacchetrà, Marco waits. He chooses only the best clusters, then lays them on bamboo racks to dry slowly for months. The grapes will lose more than half their water weight, concentrating sugars and flavors into something rare and precious. It's wine made the way it was five hundred years ago—which is to say, with more faith than efficiency.

body.quote: I remember my first vendemmia when I was seven. My nonna handed me a pair of scissors and pointed to the low vines I could reach. By noon, my fingers were sticky with grape juice and my back ached, but I felt like I'd been let in on an important secret. That evening, all the families gathered for a long table dinner in the piazza—pasta, wine, laughter echoing off the stone buildings. I understood then that the harvest wasn't just about grapes. It was about belonging to something older than yourself.
body.author: Giulia Rossi

body.markdown: December brings rain and the work shifts from vines to walls. The muretti a secco require constant maintenance—stones shift, sections collapse after heavy weather, and each one must be rebuilt by hand the old way. Marco spends these short days doing repairs, occasionally joined by volunteers from a local preservation group trying to save these historic terraces from abandonment. Inside the cantina, last year's Sciacchetrà continues its slow transformation in small oak barrels. The smell is intoxicating—dried apricots, honey, almonds, sea salt. Some barrels hold wine that won't be bottled for another two years. Patience, again. Always patience.

If you've never tasted Sciacchetrà, it's difficult to explain. It's a dessert wine, technically, but calling it that feels inadequate. The name might come from the dialect phrase "sciacca e trà"—press and pull—referring to the effort needed to extract juice from the dried grapes. Others say it derives from an ancient word for precious. Both feel true.

The traditional method requires harvesting the best Bosco, Albarola, and Vermentino clusters, then drying them on bamboo racks for three to four months. As the grapes shrivel, the sugars concentrate intensely. When Marco finally presses them in January, the yield is tiny—barely a few bottles per vine. The resulting wine is amber-gold, viscous, complex. You taste the stone terraces, the sea air, the centuries of careful hands. It pairs beautifully with local almond biscotti or aged cheeses, but honestly, it's best sipped slowly on its own while watching the sun set over these impossible vineyards. A small glass costs what seems expensive until you understand what went into making it. Then it feels like a bargain for holding this much history in your hand.

body.title: The Work Continues
body.content:
Marco's son is learning the terraces now, riding the trenino up after school, understanding through sore muscles and dirt under his fingernails what his inheritance really means. Whether he'll continue this work in twenty years is an open question. The economics are challenging. The labor is unrelenting. Climate change is already shifting harvest dates and rainfall patterns.

But for now, the vines continue their ancient rhythm above Manarola. The muretti a secco still hold back the earth and time. And every autumn, the trenino climbs the terraces carrying empty crates up and the promise of another vintage down.
